Changelog

Source: NEWS.md

ggBoostedTrees 0.10.1

boostmtree backend

  • Remotes: installs boostmtree 2.0.13 from the CCF fork (v2.0.13-ccf), and the README’s backend install line names that tag. The Imports: floor stays at 2.0.1. The fork’s releases since 2.0.8:

    • 2.0.9 holds about 60% to 70% less memory per boosting step in a fitted object.
    • 2.0.10 fixes predict() and partial.plot() stopping with “subscript out of bounds” on a fit with na.action = "na.omit" when a row of x has a missing covariate, and rejects a bad boostmtree.control(cv.cores = ) before the first tree.
    • 2.0.11 makes partial.plot() predict only at the time points it plots, and walks each step’s out-of-bag list once in a cross-validated prediction instead of scanning it for every subject.
    • 2.0.13 fixes a fixed boostmtree.control(seed = ) drawing the same subsample for every tree. With cv.flag = TRUE about 60% of subjects were never out of bag, and their fitted trajectory was a flat line at the mean response of the other subjects; the cross-validated error, m.opt and grow-object importance were computed from the rest.

  • The test fixtures are refitted with 2.0.13; the reference fit now grows M = 100, because the honest cross-validated error was still falling at 50 (m.opt is 88).

  • gg_boost_trajectory(), and so gg_boost_calibration(), warn when a cross-validated boostmtree fit records subjects that were never out of bag by m.opt, read from the fit’s own out-of-bag record (gamma.i.list), and name the cause. A flat trajectory alone does not warn: a fit with an intercept-only time design (d = 0) is flat by construction. Both document that such a fit stores out-of-bag predictions in mu, not the in-sample fit.

Variable importance

  • The gg_boost_vimp() plot is redrawn as a dot chart: one panel for main effects and one for interactions with time, sharing a variable axis and an importance scale. Every value sits at its signed importance. Values right of a grey noise band are filled dots on a stem, values inside it hollow. An interaction panel with nothing outside the band says “None detectable”, where the old bar chart drew an empty panel. The overall time effect, previously dropped, is reported in the caption.

  • New boost_shadow(x, id, k = 5) appends k shadow copies of every covariate, each shuffled between subjects, to give variable importance a noise reference measured in the fit itself. gg_boost_vimp() gains a logical shadow column that flags them by name.

  • The noise band comes from the shadows: in each panel it runs up to the largest importance any shadow reached (or zero). Shadows set the band but are not drawn. The band is a reference, not a test with a known error rate: shadows in a copy share one subject shuffle and keep the covariates’ correlations, and a covariate with no effect of its own can clear the band when it is correlated with one that has an effect. A fit without shadows draws no band and no detectable-or-not verdict, and the caption says so. A band from the largest negative importance was tried and dropped: with every tree drawing its own subsample, negatives become rare as boosting increases while a pure-noise covariate scored as high as 0.57.

Other figures

  • New gg_boost_prediction(fit, time) predicts every subject’s response at one time from predict.boostmtree() at m.opt, with the subject’s covariates, and plot(gg, covariate = ) draws the predictions against one covariate with a loess smoother. It refuses a time outside the observed follow-up, multi-response fits and BoostMLR fits.

  • The gg_boost_error() plot’s caption reports convergence: the optimal iteration against the number grown, and the error’s relative change over the last quarter of the iterations. An optimum at the last iteration with a change of a percent or so means the curve has flattened; a steep fall means refit with more iterations or a larger learning rate. Turn it off with convergence = FALSE.

Documentation

  • New article, Four Figures From One boostmtree Fit, builds the subject trajectories, variable importance, a partial effect over time and a landmark-time prediction from one fit with shadow covariates, and says how to read each. It starts by reading the error path for convergence, and says that a verdict near the edge of the band can change between runs of vimp.boostmtree().

  • The getting-started vignette fits M = 200 iterations instead of 50, so its error path levels off before the last iteration as its own advice asks, and reads the convergence caption. It seeds with set.seed() alone.

ggBoostedTrees 0.10.0

  • The plot snapshot tests skip when vdiffr is not installed instead of failing, and patchwork, which nothing uses, leaves Suggests. Both from the CRAN Cookbook audit for this release.

  • The README’s section on what cv.flag = TRUE costs gains timings and peak memory from a server, measured at 10 steps, by subjects and cores, and says that memory, not speed, limits the cores on a large fit: the parallel share levels off near 80%. It says the fit’s memory also grows with the number of steps, so the 10-step figures do not bound a longer fit. It drops the claim that the share keeps rising with the number of subjects, which the server measurements did not bear out past about 1,000, and corrects the simulated data’s visits per subject from 5 to about 9.

  • The README adds a measured full run at study size (1,391 subjects, 4,771 visits, 1,000 steps, 8 cores) on boostmtree 2.0.7 and 2.0.8: partial effects fell from 94 minutes and 70.0 GiB of session memory to 32 minutes and 11.3 GiB, with identical results.

  • Remotes: installs boostmtree 2.0.8 from the CCF fork (v2.0.8-ccf), and the README’s backend install line names that tag. The Imports: floor stays at 2.0.1. Since 2.0.4, the fork’s releases have made long fits faster and smaller without changing their results:

    • 2.0.5 makes an ordinal fit’s cross-validation about 23% faster (600 subjects, 4 cores).
    • 2.0.6 stores the cross-validation state as one vector per subject, so each forked worker holds about a quarter of the memory it did: on a server at 4,000 subjects, 8 and 16 cores now finish where 2.0.4 ran out of memory.
    • 2.0.7 runs each forked worker on one BLAS thread. On a server whose R links a multithreaded OpenBLAS, 2.0.6’s workers each started a thread per CPU and overloaded the machine: at 1,000 subjects on 4 cores, 2.0.7 took 616 s where 2.0.6 took 1,488 s.
    • 2.0.8 makes partial effects walk the boosting steps one at a time instead of holding every step for every subject at once. On a synthetic ordinal fit one partial.plot() call fell from 87 s and 4.5 GB to 2.4 s and 0.4 GB, and it adds a progress callback to boostmtree() and partial.plot().

ggBoostedTrees 0.9.3

  • The README’s Installation section now leads with hvtiR::install(), which installs the whole HVTI R family in one call, and then gives pak::pak("ehrlinger/ggBoostedTrees") for this package alone.

  • Remotes: installs boostmtree 2.0.4 from the CCF fork (v2.0.4-ccf), and the README’s backend install line names that tag. 2.0.4 adds boostmtree.control(cv.cores = ), which runs the cross-validated fit’s out-of-bag update on several cores, and is about 30% faster on one core; the fit is identical to 2.0.3’s. The Imports: floor stays at 2.0.1, because nothing in this package uses the new argument.

  • The README and the getting-started vignette say what cv.flag = TRUE costs: cross-validation’s time grows with the square of the number of subjects, with measured timings, and boostmtree 2.0.4’s boostmtree.control(cv.cores = ) runs it on several cores without changing the fit.

ggBoostedTrees 0.9.2

  • DESCRIPTION now declares the Quarto command line tool in SystemRequirements, which the new vignette needs to build.

  • New overview vignette, vignette("ggBoostedTrees"), walks one small simulated boostmtree fit through every figure the package draws, in the order you would look at them. On the pkgdown site, the article puts the table of contents on the left, as in the other HVTI packages.

ggBoostedTrees 0.9.1

  • Remotes: now pins the boostmtree fork at v2.0.3-ccf (was v2.0.2-ccf). That release only drops an unused parallel import; the cv.flag fix came in 2.0.2, so the boostmtree (>= 2.0.1) floor is unchanged. Downstream packages that pin their own boostmtree ref can now move to v2.0.3-ccf without handing pak two refs for one package.

ggBoostedTrees 0.9.0

  • gg_boost_vimp() accepts a BoostMLR predict object made with predictBoostMLR(..., importance = TRUE). BoostMLR splits the covariate-time interaction over its time intervals; these are summed to one interaction value per covariate, and the per-interval matrices are kept in the interaction.by.interval attribute (#9).
  • New boostmlr_partial() computes BoostMLR partial effects for one or more covariates, naming the covariates and responses that BoostMLR::partial.BoostMLR() leaves unnamed. gg_boost_effect() accepts the result and extracts the lowess-smoothed curves, one block per response. All six figures now accept a BoostMLR fit. BoostMLR support remains partial: marginal effects and joint importance are not supported (#9).
  • gg_boost_effect() now accepts the partial.plot() and marginal.plot() output of a multi-response (ordinal or nominal) boostmtree fit, which it previously refused. Every result gains a response factor, labelled from the object’s response.labels; a single-response fit is labelled "response" and otherwise unchanged. autoplot() facets by response, as a grid of response by variable when there are several of each (#19).

ggBoostedTrees 0.0.7

  • The README function reference now lists gg_boost_calibration() and its autoplot() method alongside the other shipped figure-data objects.
  • New gg_boost_calibration() compares observed and fitted values over follow-up. Observations are binned by time into equal-count bins, and each bin reports the observed mean with a 95% interval, the fitted mean at the same observations, and how many observations and distinct subjects stand behind it. It accepts boostmtree and BoostMLR fits.
  • Supplying a boostmtree predict object as pred adds the cohort mean curve. A predict object made with tm and id is refused, because each subject is then predicted at its own times and a mean across subjects would change composition along the curve.
  • The renderer draws each bin’s time span, so a thin tail shows as a long late bin.

ggBoostedTrees 0.0.6

  • BoostMLR fits are now accepted by gg_boost_trajectory(), gg_boost_error() and gg_boost_path(). Adding the backend required extractor methods only; no renderer changed, which is what the tidy intermediate exists to guarantee.
  • BoostMLR selects no optimal boosting iteration, so gg_boost_error() flags none for that backend rather than deriving one.
  • BoostMLR’s Lambda_List holds per-iteration basis coefficients rather than a scalar smoothing parameter, so gg_boost_path() offers rho and phi for that backend and says so if lambda is requested.
  • gg_boost_vimp() and gg_boost_effect() remain boostmtree only.
  • gg_boost_error() refuses use.rmse = FALSE on a BoostMLR fit, by name or by position: that backend records no y.sd, so its Error_Rate cannot be unstandardized. The generic declares use.rmse as its second formal, so the positional form is valid syntax, and it previously fell through and returned standardized values to a caller who had asked for the other scale. use.rmse = TRUE is accepted, being the default and the scale BoostMLR already returns, so a caller that always passes the argument runs against either backend unchanged.
  • autoplot.gg_boost_trajectory() accepts a repeated subject identifier in subset rather than failing with an internal factor level [2] is duplicated. The caller’s ordering still determines the factor levels.
  • gg_boost_path()’s boostmtree method validates parameters the same way its BoostMLR sibling and gg_boost_vimp()’s components argument do: an empty vector is rejected and duplicates are de-duplicated rather than reaching an opaque factor() error.

ggBoostedTrees 0.0.5

  • gg_boost_effect() now handles factor covariates. It previously coerced their labels with as.numeric(), producing an all-NA covariate column and a blank figure. The contract gains an x_label column, and the renderer draws discrete covariates as points on a labelled axis.
  • An object mixing continuous and discrete covariates is refused with guidance, since one figure permits only one scale type per aesthetic.
  • gg_boost_vimp() validates components: an empty vector is rejected and duplicates are de-duplicated rather than reaching an opaque factor() error.
  • Corrected the description of marginal.plot()’s $data, which holds unsmoothed fitted predictions rather than raw observations.

ggBoostedTrees 0.0.4

  • gg_boost_vimp() and plot()/autoplot() for variable importance, covering both the main effect of each covariate and its interaction with time. The axis is labelled with the metric recorded on the source object rather than a hard-coded string.
  • gg_boost_effect() and plot()/autoplot() for partial and marginal covariate effects over time, as one class distinguished by kind.
  • Neither partial.plot() nor marginal.plot() computes a confidence interval, so gg_boost_effect() reports none.

ggBoostedTrees 0.0.3

  • gg_boost_trajectory() and plot()/autoplot() for observed and fitted subject trajectories over time. Rows are sorted within subject, because boostmtree stores observations in input order and a line drawn from that order zigzags.
  • The trajectory renderer thins large cohorts with subset and n_max, and scales transparency to the number of subjects drawn so that an overplotted cohort reads as a density.

ggBoostedTrees 0.0.2

  • gg_boost_error() and plot()/autoplot() for the boosting error path, marking the cross-validated optimal iteration. Requires a fit grown with cv.flag = TRUE.
  • gg_boost_path() and plot()/autoplot() for the rho, phi and lambda parameter paths.
  • autoplot() on a boostmtree fit as a shortcut to the error path.

ggBoostedTrees 0.0.1

  • Package skeleton, shared utilities, and the testthat scaffold.
